The Vulgate is a Latin translation of the Hebrew Bible and New Testament completed by Jerome between three hundred ninety and four hundred five of the common era. It was commissioned by Pope Damasus to provide a unified, authoritative scripture for the Western church. It became the official Bible of the Roman Catholic Church for over fifteen hundred years and shaped Christian theology, liturgy, and Latin itself through its phrasings.

Pope Damasus the First commissioned the work to replace the Old Latin translations, which were fragmentary and inconsistent across different scriptural manuscripts. Jerome was a Church Father and linguist who translated the Hebrew Bible directly from Hebrew, not from the Septuagint, and revised the New Testament from Greek manuscripts. He completed this meticulous work over fifteen years, comparing manuscripts and consulting Jewish scholars to understand difficult Hebrew words. The term Vulgate comes from the Latin vulgata, meaning common or common tongue, reflecting its purpose: scripture in the language of everyday Latin-speaking Christians.

Jerome's translation was officially adopted as the exclusive biblical text of the Catholic Church at the Council of Trent, which met from fifteen forty-five to fifteen sixty-three, cementing its authority for four centuries. Medieval scholars added the fourfold method of biblical interpretation—literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical—to commentaries on the Vulgate, shaping Christian exegesis. The Sixtine edition of fifteen ninety and the Clementine edition of fifteen ninety-two standardized the Vulgate text for the modern Catholic Church. During the Reformation, Protestant translators like Tyndale and Luther used the Vulgate as a reference alongside the original Hebrew and Greek.
